ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Surveys and Experiments of the Graduate School of Arts and Letters, Tohoku University (20260410).

Fifteen participants completed two experiments using a spatial-cuing task in which central arrow cues predicted the side on which targets would appear at 3°, 10°, and 40° eccentricity, with double-headed arrows serving as neutral cues.
No participants were excluded from the analyses.
Participants were 18 to 25 years old (M = 22.38, SD = 1.93); five were male and 10 were female.

An a priori power analysis using G*Power 3.1.9.7 indicated that 15 participants were required to detect the main effect of validity in a repeated-measures analysis of variance (f = 0.40, α = .05, power = .90).
The same 15 participants completed both Experiments 1 and 2 over four nonconsecutive days.
Experiment order was counterbalanced: eight participants completed the sequence 1-2-2-1, and seven completed 2-1-1-2.
All participants provided written informed consent and received monetary compensation.
Participants were instructed to maintain central fixation and to report the target side using the corresponding arrow key as quickly and accurately as possible.
In catch trials, no target appeared, and participants were instructed to withhold their response.
No participants were excluded from the analyses.

text.text: Endogenous spatial attention allows observers to prioritize behaviorally relevant locations, but whether it remains effective in far-peripheral vision, where the cortical representation of a given stimulus is markedly reduced, is not fully understood.

The present study examined whether endogenous spatial attention produces reaction-time facilitation at 40° eccentricity and whether the magnitude of this facilitation varies with eccentricity and stimulus scaling based on cortical magnification.

Fifteen participants completed two experiments using a spatial-cuing task in which central arrow cues predicted the side on which targets would appear at 3°, 10°, and 40° eccentricity, with double-headed arrows serving as neutral cues.
In Experiment 1, target stimuli were identical in physical size across eccentricities.
In Experiment 2, stimulus size was adjusted according to the cortical magnification factor to partially reduce eccentricity-dependent differences in cortical representation.
In both experiments, responses were fastest in the valid condition, intermediate in the neutral condition, and slowest in the invalid condition.
A reliable cuing effect was observed at 40° eccentricity in both experiments.
The magnitude of the cuing effect did not reliably differ across eccentricities in either experiment, nor between the unscaled and M-scaled conditions at 40°.
These findings indicate that endogenous spatial attention remains behaviorally effective in far-peripheral vision at 40° eccentricity.
Peripheral vision plays an important role in monitoring the surrounding environment and guiding behavior in real-world tasks [1].
text.formatted: Peripheral vision plays an important role in monitoring the surrounding environment and guiding behavior in real-world tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: However, information in the peripheral visual field is subject to substantial sensory constraints.
The human visual system exhibits marked spatial inhomogeneity, with spatial resolution and contrast sensitivity declining substantially as retinal eccentricity increases [2, 3, 4].
text.formatted: The human visual system exhibits marked spatial inhomogeneity, with spatial resolution and contrast sensitivity declining substantially as retinal eccentricity increases <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: This eccentricity-dependent decline is partly rooted in the anatomical organization of the retina, as cone photoreceptor and retinal ganglion-cell densities vary with distance from the fovea [5, 6].
text.formatted: This eccentricity-dependent decline is partly rooted in the anatomical organization of the retina, as cone photoreceptor and retinal ganglion-cell densities vary with distance from the fovea <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: At more eccentric locations, signals from multiple photoreceptors are pooled by retinal circuitry into the output of individual retinal ganglion cells, reducing spatial sampling resolution [6].
text.formatted: At more eccentric locations, signals from multiple photoreceptors are pooled by retinal circuitry into the output of individual retinal ganglion cells, reducing spatial sampling resolution <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Eccentricity-dependent inhomogeneity is also evident at the cortical level.

In the primary visual cortex, foveal and parafoveal inputs occupy a disproportionately large cortical area, whereas progressively less cortical area is devoted to more peripheral visual-field locations [7].
text.formatted: In the primary visual cortex, foveal and parafoveal inputs occupy a disproportionately large cortical area, whereas progressively less cortical area is devoted to more peripheral visual-field locations <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: This variation in cortical representation across eccentricity is commonly described in terms of the cortical magnification factor (CMF), often expressed as the amount of cortical distance devoted to one degree of visual angle [8].
text.formatted: This variation in cortical representation across eccentricity is commonly described in terms of the cortical magnification factor (CMF), often expressed as the amount of cortical distance devoted to one degree of visual angle <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Endogenous spatial attention provides a potential mechanism for selectively prioritizing behaviorally relevant information under the sensory constraints of peripheral vision.
Based on current goals and predictive information, observers can direct attention in advance to possible target locations without overt eye movements [9, 10].
text.formatted: Based on current goals and predictive information, observers can direct attention in advance to possible target locations without overt eye movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: In spatial cuing paradigms, this anticipatory prioritization typically facilitates responses to targets appearing at expected locations.
Such top-down prioritization may be particularly relevant for visual processing at large eccentricities, where sensory representations are increasingly constrained.
However, the extent to which endogenous spatial attention remains effective in farperipheral vision is not fully understood.

Far-peripheral vision has received relatively limited attention in studies of visual attention, partly because large eccentricities are difficult to accommodate using standard laboratory displays [11].
text.formatted: Far-peripheral vision has received relatively limited attention in studies of visual attention, partly because large eccentricities are difficult to accommodate using standard laboratory displays <ref type="bibr">[11]</ref>.

text.text: In particular, endogenous pre-cuing has rarely been examined beyond approximately 20° eccentricity.

Feng and Spence [12] provided an important exception by examining endogenous pre-cuing at eccentricities up to 30° and showed that predictive spatial cues can modulate visual performance across a relatively broad range of eccentricities.
text.formatted: Feng and Spence <ref type="bibr">[12]</ref> provided an important exception by examining endogenous pre-cuing at eccentricities up to 30° and showed that predictive spatial cues can modulate visual performance across a relatively broad range of eccentricities.

text.text: Whether goal-directed spatial prioritization extends beyond the previously examined range to 40°, where sensory constraints are even more pronounced, has yet to be established.
A further issue is whether the behavioral effect of endogenous attention depends on eccentricity-dependent differences in cortical representation.
Because cortical magnification decreases with eccentricity, the same physical stimulus size produces substantially different cortical representation across eccentricities.
This raises the possibility that the behavioral expression of attentional prioritization at far-peripheral locations is constrained by the limited cortical representation of the target.

M-scaling provides a means of examining this possibility by adjusting stimulus size according to the cortical magnification factor, thereby partially reducing eccentricity-dependent differences in cortical representation [8].
text.formatted: M-scaling provides a means of examining this possibility by adjusting stimulus size according to the cortical magnification factor, thereby partially reducing eccentricity-dependent differences in cortical representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: A related theoretical possibility is that endogenous attention serves a possible compensatory role under the greater sensory constraints of far-peripheral vision.

If endogenous attention compensates for increasing sensory constraints with eccentricity, attentional facilitation may become greater at far-peripheral locations, where visual information is more limited.

However, such a facilitation might be difficult to observe behaviorally if the limited cortical representation of an unscaled far-peripheral target constrains the expression of attentional facilitation.
If this were the case, a larger attentional benefit at 40° might become more evident after M-scaling.

The present study examined whether endogenous spatial attention produces reaction-time facilitation at 40° eccentricity and whether its behavioral effect varies with eccentricity-dependent differences in cortical representation.
In Experiment 1, target stimuli of identical physical size were presented at 3°, 10°, and 40° eccentricity to test whether predictive spatial cues facilitate responses even in far-peripheral vision.
In Experiment 2, stimulus size was adjusted according to the cortical magnification factor to partially reduce eccentricity-dependent differences in cortical representation.
This allowed us to examine whether the pattern of endogenous cueing observed under unscaled conditions changed when this source of eccentricity-dependent variation was reduced.

We predicted that predictive spatial cues would shorten reaction times at 40° as well as at 3° and 10° and examined whether any eccentricity-dependent increase in attentional benefit would become evident when differences in cortical representation were partially reduced by Mscaling.
Fifteen students from Tohoku University participated in Experiment 1.
All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were right-handed.
No participants were excluded from the analyses.
Participants were 18 to 25 years old (M = 22.38, SD = 1.93); five were male and 10 were female.

An a priori power analysis using G*Power 3.1.9.7 indicated that 15 participants were required to detect the main effect of validity in a repeated-measures analysis of variance (f = 0.40, α = .05, power = .90).
The same 15 participants completed both Experiments 1 and 2 over four nonconsecutive days.
Experiment order was counterbalanced: eight participants completed the sequence 1-2-2-1, and seven completed 2-1-1-2.
All participants provided written informed consent and received monetary compensation.
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Surveys and Experiments of the Graduate School of Arts and Letters, Tohoku University (20260410).

Stimuli were generated and controlled using MATLAB R2024a (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA) with the Cogent 2000 Graphics toolbox (version 1.33; developed at the Laboratory of Neurobiology, University College London).
They were projected onto a 100-inch screen using a projector (BenQ TH671ST; 1920 × 1080-pixel resolution; 60-Hz refresh rate).
At the viewing distance of 113 cm, the projected image subtended approximately 92.2° horizontally.
Stimulus luminance was gamma-corrected based on measurements obtained with a BM-7 Fast luminance colorimeter (Topcon, Tokyo, Japan).
Participants sat in a dark room with their head stabilized on a chin rest.

Experiment 2 showed a reliable cuing effect under M-scaled stimulus conditions, including at 40°.
Reaction times were fastest in the valid condition, intermediate in the neutral condition, and slowest in the invalid condition.
Accuracy remained high and the faster responses in the valid condition were not accompanied by reduced accuracy, making a speed-accuracy trade-off unlikely.
Importantly, the Eccentricity × Validity interaction was not significant, providing no evidence that the magnitude of the cuing effect differed across eccentricities under Mscaled conditions.

Moreover, the direct comparison of the 40° condition across experiments showed that M-scaling substantially reduced overall reaction times but did not reliably alter the magnitude of the cuing effect.

Thus, although reducing eccentricity-dependent differences in cortical representation affected overall response speed at 40°, the behavioral effect of endogenous spatial attention remained relatively stable.
Together with Experiment 1, these findings indicate that endogenous spatial attention remains effective at 40° under both unscaled and M-scaled stimulus conditions.

The present study examined whether endogenous spatial attention remains effective at 40° eccentricity and whether its effect changes when eccentricity-dependent differences in cortical representation are partially reduced.
Across both experiments, responses were consistently fastest in the valid condition, intermediate in the neutral condition, and slowest in the invalid condition.
This cuing pattern was reliably observed in the analyses restricted to 40° and remained present when stimulus size was adjusted according to the cortical magnification factor.
The reliable cuing effect observed at 40° extends previous evidence that endogenous spatial attention can operate across a wide range of eccentricities.
Previous research had shown that endogenous pre-cuing can modulate visual performance at eccentricities up to approximately 30° [12].

The present findings extend this evidence by demonstrating that predictive spatial cues can effectively prioritize behaviorally relevant locations even at 40° eccentricity, where sensory constraints are more pronounced.
Across the two experiments, the cuing effect did not reliably increase at 40° eccentricity.
In Experiment 1, targets were physically identical across eccentricities, and the magnitude of the cuing effect did not reliably increase with eccentricity.

Because physically identical stimuli produce smaller cortical representations at larger eccentricities, however, it remained possible that the behavioral expression of attentional prioritization at 40° was constrained by the limited cortical representation of the far-peripheral stimulus.
Experiment 2 therefore used M-scaling to partially reduce eccentricity-dependent differences in cortical representation.
Nevertheless, the cuing effect again remained robust at 40° without reliably increasing relative to less eccentric locations.
A direct comparison of the 40° condition across experiments further showed that the magnitude of the cuing effect did not reliably differ between the unscaled and M-scaled conditions.
Taken together, reducing this major source of eccentricity-dependent variation did not substantially alter the pattern of endogenous spatial prioritization.
This pattern provided no evidence that a larger farperipheral attentional benefit had been masked by the limited cortical representation of the unscaled stimulus.
At the same time, it provided no evidence for a compensatory increase in reaction-time benefit toward the far periphery under the present task conditions.
The relation between eccentricity and the magnitude of the cuing effect may nevertheless depend on task characteristics and the type of attention involved.
Feng and Spence [12] reported larger endogenous pre-cuing effects on accuracy at greater eccentricities in a more demanding target-localization task with distractors.
In the present study, observers were required only to localize a high-contrast target to the left or right of fixation, and accuracy remained high across eccentricities.

text.text: One limitation is that fixation was maintained through instruction and head stabilization but was not objectively verified using eye tracking.

Small gaze deviations could therefore have altered the effective retinal eccentricity of the targets, although they would be unlikely to eliminate the far-peripheral status of targets presented at 40°.
Future studies incorporating continuous eye-position monitoring would provide a more stringent test of covert endogenous spatial attention at large eccentricities.
Taken together, the present study demonstrated that predictive spatial cues effectively modulate responses even at 40° eccentricity.
This cuing effect was observed under both unscaled and M-scaled stimulus conditions, indicating that endogenous spatial attention remains behaviorally effective in far-peripheral vision.

The persistence of the cuing effect across these conditions suggests that far-peripheral endogenous spatial prioritization is relatively robust to the source of eccentricity-dependent variation in cortical representation manipulated by M-scaling.

At the same time, the cuing effect was not reliably greater at 40° than at less eccentric locations, providing no evidence for a compensatory increase in reaction-time benefit toward the far periphery under the present task conditions.
Rather, these findings suggest that endogenous spatial attention prioritizes behaviorally relevant locations across a broad range of eccentricities including far-peripheral vision.

Stimuli were presented on a gray background (92.05 cd/m²).
A black fixation cross (0.9° × 0.9°; 0.1119 cd/m²) was presented at the center of the screen.
Six black square placeholders (2.5° × 2.5°) were displayed continuously throughout each trial, with one placeholder at 3°, 10°, and 40° eccentricity to the left and right of fixation.
The targets were achromatic Gaussian blobs generated within a 51 × 51-pixel (2.5° × 2.5°) image, with an SD of 9 pixels (0.43°) and were presented at the center of one of the placeholders.

Luminance varied smoothly from the gray background (92.05 cd/m²) toward either white (180.6 cd/m²) or black (0.1119 cd/m²) at the center, producing positive-and negative-contrast targets, which occurred equally often across trials.
Target size was identical across eccentricities.
The cue was a black symbolic arrow (0.3° × 0.8°) presented at fixation.
A rightward or leftward arrow indicated the likely target side, whereas a double-headed arrow served as the neutral cue.

Previous studies using exogenous cues have demonstrated attentional facilitation at far-peripheral locations, including eccentricities of approximately 56-60° [11,13].
